usage: 서로 (each other) is the textbook partner word here; it frames cooperation as mutual, not one-sided.
긴밀히 (closely/tightly) is the standard adverb in news and business; 'work closely together'.
협력 + 업체 is a fixed business noun for a contracted partner; shows the bare noun 협력 in compounds.
Set closing line in emails and notices; more institutional than the warm, personal 도와줘서 고마워요.
examples: 우리 같이 협력해요.
Let's cooperate together.
Simple 요-form invitation; 같이 (together) makes the joint effort explicit between equals.
두 회사가 협력해서 새 제품을 개발했어요.
The two companies collaborated to develop a new product.
협력해서 = 'by cooperating', chaining the joint effort to its result; very common in work and business talk.
이번 프로젝트는 옆 팀과 긴밀히 협력해야 성공할 수 있습니다.
This project can only succeed if we cooperate closely with the next team.
Real workplace register: partner marked with 과, 긴밀히 collocates, 협력해야 sets a condition for success.
nuance: 협력하다 (協力, literally '협 join forces + 력 strength') means two or more parties pooling effort toward a shared goal, so it fits teams, companies, departments, and governments rather than one friend doing you a casual favor. The dividing line to memorize: 돕다 / 도와주다 is one-directional help ('you help me'), while 협력하다 is mutual, goal-oriented teamwork ('we work together as partners'); 협조하다 is the close cousin meaning 'cooperate by going along with a request' (협조 부탁드립니다 = please cooperate with our request) and is softer and more procedural than the strategic 협력하다. The partner is marked with 와/과 or 하고 (옆 팀과 협력해요), it habitually pairs with 서로, 긴밀히, and 적극적으로, and the bare noun is everywhere: 국제 협력, 협력 업체, 협력 관계. Being a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly to 협력해요 / 협력했어요, and negatives usually split the noun off (협력 안 해요). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 협력하다 whenever you'd say 'help' in English — for 'help me move this desk' you must say 도와주세요, never 협력해 주세요.

mistakes: Using 협력하다 for a small one-off favor: 'help me carry this' is 이것 좀 도와주세요, not 협력해 주세요 — 협력하다 needs a joint, goal-directed effort, not single-person assistance.

usage: 치열하다 (fierce, cut-throat) is the signature adverb for 경쟁하다; describes tough, no-quarter rivalry.
을/를 두고 (with N at stake) is the natural frame for a prize, spot, or position people contend for.
선의의 (good-willed) + 경쟁 is a set phrase for healthy rivalry that pushes both sides to improve.
Common reassurance; the rival takes 와/과 (친구와 경쟁할 필요 없어요 = no need to compete with your friend).
examples: 우리 누가 빠른지 경쟁해요.
Let's compete to see who's faster.
Light, playful use; 누가 ~지 sets up the thing being contested between two people.
요즘 회사들이 가격으로 심하게 경쟁하고 있어요.
These days companies are competing hard on price.
(으)로 marks what they compete on; 경쟁하고 있다 (ongoing) frames it as a current, live situation.
같은 자리를 두고 여러 명이 치열하게 경쟁했어요.
Several people competed fiercely for the same position.
Full real-life pattern: N을/를 두고 + 치열하게 + 경쟁하다, the way news reports describe a contest.
nuance: 경쟁하다 (競爭, '競 vie + 爭 contend') describes rivalry in which parties try to outdo one another for the same prize, market, or position, and its tone runs from neutral and sporty to tense and cut-throat depending on context. The boundary worth knowing: 경쟁하다 is contending against a rival, whereas 겨루다 is a more physical 'pit your skill/strength against' (used for matches and martial arts), and 다투다 leans toward quarreling or squabbling. Grammar is the trap zone here: the rival is marked with 와/과 (옆 가게와 경쟁해요), and what is at stake takes 을/를 두고, never a plain object on 경쟁 itself. It collocates with 치열하게, 심하게, and the set phrase 선의의 경쟁, and the noun saturates daily life: 경쟁률 (competition ratio), 입시 경쟁 (exam competition), 경쟁사 (a competitor), 경쟁력 (competitiveness). As a regular 하다-verb it gives 경쟁해요 / 경쟁했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 경쟁 like the English noun 'the competition' that you 'win' — Korean separates the act (경쟁) from the result, so you win 'in' the competition (경쟁에서 이기다), you don't 'beat the competition' as 경쟁을 이기다.

english: to participate / to take part in
usage: to take part in an event
참여하다 takes 에 for the activity you join: 토론에 참여해요 = I take part in the discussion.
적극적으로 (actively, proactively) is the most natural adverb; stresses real involvement, not token presence.
to take part in a survey
Shows 참여하다 covering contribution to a vote, poll, or survey — you add input, not just attend.
Standard call-to-action in notices; asks people to get involved and contribute, not merely turn up.
examples: 저도 그 모임에 참여하고 싶어요.
I want to take part in that gathering too.
Basic 에 marking plus 고 싶다; 참여하다 already implies you'll actually join in, not just watch.
이번 봉사 활동에 적극적으로 참여했어요.
I actively took part in this volunteer activity.
적극적으로 collocates strongly; 참여하다 stresses hands-on involvement rather than mere attendance.
회의에 참여는 했지만 의견은 한마디도 안 냈어요.
I took part in the meeting but didn't say a single word.
Splitting 참여 + 는 + 했다 adds contrast, showing 참여하다 is active involvement you can still hold back within.
nuance: 참여하다 (參與, '參 take part + 與 join in') means to actively take part in and contribute to an activity, event, or process, so its core is involvement, not physical presence. The single most useful contrast for a learner: 참석하다 (出席) is simply attending — being bodily present at a meeting, wedding, or ceremony — whereas 참여하다 means you actually engage and add something. You 참석 a friend's wedding (you show up and sit there), but you 참여 a project or campaign (you roll up your sleeves); a related word 가담하다 is 'join in' with a negative slant (joining a crime or a fight). What you join is marked with 에 (행사에 참여하다), and it pairs habitually with 적극적으로 and the bare noun in 참여율 (participation rate), 시민 참여 (citizen participation), 참여형 (participatory). As a regular 하다-verb it is 참여해요 / 참여했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is using one word for both 'attend' and 'participate' the way English does — if you only mean you were physically there, say 참석했어요; save 참여했어요 for when you genuinely took part.

Treating 참여하다 and 참석하다 as freely interchangeable. They differ in meaning: 참석 = be present, 참여 = get involved, and picking the wrong one misstates how engaged you were.

usage: to take responsibility to the very end
끝까지 (all the way to the end) is the signature partner; means seeing it through, not bailing out.
to be answerable for the outcome
The matter takes 을/를: 결과를 / 사고를 / 일을 책임지다 — what you own up to is a direct object.
Strong promise of accountability; the -ㄹ게요 pledge form is how you volunteer to own an outcome.
to be unable to take responsibility
Note the negative potential; 책임 + 지다 splits to 책임 못 져요 / 책임지지 못해요 in everyday speech.
examples: 제 일은 제가 책임져요.
I take responsibility for my own work.
Clean 져요 form; shows the 지다 stem contracting and the matter (일) taken as object with 을 dropped.
누가 이 사고를 책임질 거예요?
Who's going to take responsibility for this accident?
책임지다 + 을/를: 사고를 책임지다 = be answerable for the accident; future 거예요 presses for ownership.
이 일은 제가 맡았으니까 끝까지 책임지겠습니다.
I took this on, so I'll take full responsibility to the end.
Formal workplace pledge: 맡다 (take charge) sets it up, 책임지겠습니다 promises to own how it turns out.
nuance: 책임지다 is a compound of the Sino-Korean noun 책임 (責任, '責 duty + 任 charge') plus the native verb 지다 'to carry/bear', so it literally means 'to shoulder responsibility' — to take on and own the consequences of a mistake, a task, or even the care of a person. It is heavier and more accountable than 맡다 (to take charge of / be assigned): 맡다 is accepting a duty, while 책임지다 is promising to answer for the result, good or bad. It also reaches beyond fault into provision — 가족을 책임지다 means to support and care for one's family — so it overlaps emotionally with 돌보다 (to look after) in that nurturing sense. The matter takes 을/를, it collocates with 끝까지 and 확실히, and it lives in nouns like 책임감 (sense of responsibility) and 무책임 (irresponsibility). The conjugation pitfall is the key thing for English speakers: because the stem is 지다, you must contract it to 책임져요 / 책임졌어요 / 책임져 주세요 — never the literal *책임지어요 — and negatives split the noun off as 책임 안 져요.

Marking the matter with 에 (사고에 책임져요). What you take responsibility for is a direct object with 을/를: 사고를 책임져요 (or in formal writing 사고에 대해 책임지다).

english: to rely on / to lean on (emotionally)
usage: A person you lean on takes 에게/한테: 가족에게 / 친구한테 의지해요 — emotional, warm dependence.
서로 (each other) frames mutual support; 서로 의지하며 살다 = to live leaning on one another.
With a physical object for support, use 에: 벽에 / 지팡이에 의지해서 걷다 = walk leaning on it.
Common advice against leaning on someone emotionally or financially to an unhealthy degree.
examples: 나는 언니한테 많이 의지해.
I rely on my older sister a lot.
Casual 반말 with 한테; shows the everyday, intimate flavor of leaning on a close family member.
힘들 때 친구에게 의지하면 마음이 편해져요.
When times are hard, leaning on a friend makes you feel better.
에게 marks who you lean on; 의지하다 carries warm, trusting emotional dependence, not a transaction.
할머니는 지팡이에 의지해서 천천히 걸으세요.
Grandmother walks slowly, leaning on a cane.
Physical sense with 에; 의지해서 chains the support to the action of walking.
nuance: 의지하다 (依支, '依 depend + 支 prop up') means to depend on or lean on someone or something for emotional, practical, or even physical support, and it almost always carries a warm, human feeling of trust rather than cold reliance. The boundary to learn: 의지하다 is leaning on someone for support and comfort, while 믿다 is believing in or trusting them, and 기대다 is the most physical/intimate 'lean against' (you can 어깨에 기대다 lean on a shoulder, and figuratively it sounds even tenderer). A crucial particle split: a person you rely on takes 에게/한테 (부모님께 의지해요), but an object you physically lean on takes 에 (벽에 의지하다). It collocates with 서로 and 많이, and the bare noun appears in 의지가 되다 (to be a source of support). The 하다-verb conjugates regularly to 의지해요 / 의지했어요. Two pitfalls for English speakers: (1) do not mark the person with 을/를 — English 'rely on someone' tempts a direct object, but Korean needs 에게/한테; and (2) the 'let's rely' (shallWe) form is unnatural, since relying isn't something two people propose doing in concert, so treat 의지할까요? as a real question ('shall I lean on you?'), not a casual suggestion.

english: to respect / to look up to
usage: to respect from the bottom of one's heart
마음 깊이 / 진심으로 intensify it; 존경하다 is already deep, so these stress sincere admiration.
The modifier 존경하는 is a fixed, slightly formal lead-in: 존경하는 선생님 = a teacher I look up to.
존경하는 마음(으로) names the attitude behind an action: '(I did it) with a respectful heart'.
The passive 존경받다/존경을 받다 is very common: 모두에게 존경받는 분 = a person everyone looks up to.
examples: 저는 우리 할아버지를 존경해요.
I look up to my grandfather.
Plain 을/를 object; the admired person is a direct object, and the feeling is looking up to their character.
저는 늘 도전하시는 그분을 진심으로 존경해요.
I sincerely respect that person who always takes on challenges.
진심으로 collocates; the honorific 도전하시는 shows you elevate someone you 존경 with 시 inside the clause.
그렇게 끝까지 책임지시는 걸 보니 더 존경하게 됐어요.
Seeing them stay responsible to the end, I came to respect them even more.
존경하게 되다 = 'come to respect', marking a shift in feeling triggered by witnessed behavior.
nuance: 존경하다 (尊敬, '尊 honor + 敬 revere') is deep respect and admiration for a person's character, achievements, or values — looking up to an elder, mentor, hero, or role model. Two boundaries matter. First, it is far stronger and more upward-looking than 좋아하다 (to like): you can like a singer's songs (좋아하다) yet 존경 a person only for who they are. Second, and the classic mix-up, 존경하다 vs 존중하다 (尊重): you 존경 a *person* you admire, but you 존중 someone's *choices, opinions, or rights* — 다른 사람의 의견을 존중하다 (respect others' opinions), never 존경. The admired person takes 을/를, the modifier 존경하는 is a common formal lead-in, and the passive 존경받다 ('be respected') is everywhere. As a regular 하다-verb it is 존경해요 / 존경했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'respect' covers both senses at once, so learners overuse 존경하다 for everyday courtesy ('respect the rules', 'respect your privacy') where Korean needs 존중하다 — 규칙을 존중하다, not 규칙을 존경하다.

mistakes: Confusing 존경하다 with 존중하다. You 존경 a person you admire, but you 존중 a decision, opinion, or right: 의견을 존중해요, not 의견을 존경해요.
Using 존경하다 for mere liking: 'I really like this actor' is 이 배우 정말 좋아해요; 존경하다 implies looking up to someone's character, which overshoots casual fondness.
Marking the admired person with 에게/한테 (선생님에게 존경해요). The person you look up to is a direct object with 을/를: 선생님을 존경해요.

english: to ignore / to look down on
usage: 그냥 무시해 = don't even react; standard advice for shrugging off rude comments or trolls.
The 'disregard' sense: rules, warnings, red lights — 규칙을/경고를 무시하다 = flout what you should heed.
to look down on a person
The belittling sense — treating someone as beneath you; a strong, hurtful reproach toward people.
to be ignored / be looked down on
The passive is extremely common when describing being slighted: 무시당한 기분이 들었어요.
examples: 그 사람 말은 그냥 무시해.
Just ignore what that person says.
Casual 반말 advice; 무시하다 + 을/를 here is the harmless 'don't pay it any attention' sense.
빨간 신호를 무시하고 길을 건너면 정말 위험해요.
It's really dangerous to ignore a red light and cross.
Disregard-a-rule sense; 무시하고 chains the flouting to its risky consequence.
돈이 없다고 사람을 무시하면 안 돼요.
You shouldn't look down on people just because they have no money.
The belittle sense, which is offensive; 무시당하다 (to be looked down on) is its common passive partner.
nuance: 무시하다 (無視, literally '無 without + 視 looking' — 'to not look at') carries two linked senses that context decides between: (1) to ignore or disregard something — a comment, a rule, a warning, a red light — and (2) to look down on, belittle, or disrespect a person, which is quite offensive. With an inanimate target it's the neutral first sense (신호를 무시하다 = disregard the signal); with a person it usually flips to the cutting second sense (사람을 무시하다 = treat them as inferior). Distinguish it from neighbors: 무시하다 (ignore by choice / belittle) is not 모르다 (genuinely not know) and not 외면하다 (deliberately turn one's face away, look away from a problem). The target takes 을/를, it pairs with 그냥, and the passive 무시당하다 ('be slighted') is everywhere in emotional talk. The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 무시하다 just means the neutral English 'ignore' — aim it at a person and it commonly reads as 'look down on', so 나를 무시하지 마 is a forceful 'don't disrespect me', far heavier than 'don't ignore me'; if you only mean failing to notice, 무시하다 is the wrong verb entirely.

Marking the target with 에 (신호에 무시해요). What you ignore is a direct object: 신호를 무시해요, 사람을 무시해요 — always 을/를.

english: to discuss / to talk over (to decide)
usage: to talk it over with one's parents
The person you consult takes 와/과 (or 하고): you discuss *with* them to reach a decision.
The topic takes 에 대해: N에 대해 의논하다 = talk over the matter of N, often to get advice.
같이 (together) underlines the two-way nature; 혼자 정하지 말고 같이 의논해요 = let's decide jointly.
의논해 보다 = give discussing-it-over a try; used when you must consult someone before deciding.
examples: 우리 그거 같이 의논해요.
Let's talk that over together.
Simple 요-form invitation; 같이 marks it as a joint consultation, not a one-way report.
이 문제는 부모님과 의논해 보고 결정할게요.
I'll talk this over with my parents before I decide.
와/과 marks who you consult; 의논해 보고 결정하다 shows the whole point is to reach a decision.
진로에 대해 선생님과 진지하게 의논했어요.
I had a serious discussion with my teacher about my career path.
Real-life pattern: 에 대해 (topic) + 와/과 (partner) + 진지하게 + 의논하다, the way you describe seeking advice.
nuance: 의논하다 (議論, '議 deliberate + 論 discuss') is to talk something over with someone in order to reach a decision or get advice, so its essence is practical, two-way consultation, not a formal contest of ideas. Hold three neighbors apart. 의논하다 / 상의하다 both mean 'consult to decide' (상의하다 sounds a touch more formal and businesslike), so they're near-twins. 토론하다 (debate) means weighing opposing sides on an issue — public, argumentative — which 의논하다 is not. And 대화하다 (converse) is just friendly chatting with no decision at stake. The crucial particles: the person you consult takes 와/과 or 하고 (친구와 의논해요), and the topic takes 에 대해 (진로에 대해 의논해요). It pairs with 같이, 진지하게, and lives in 의논 상대 (someone to talk things over with). As a 하다-verb it is 의논해요 / 의논했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'discuss it WITH my parents' tempts you toward a 'to' marker, but the consultation partner must take 와/과, never 에게/한테 — 의논하다 is mutual, not one-directional delivery.

Using 의논하다 for a formal debate of opposing views; that is 토론하다. 의논하다 is consulting to decide, so a panel or classroom argument calls for 토론하다.
Treating 의논하다 as plain chatting. If there's no decision or advice at stake, 'let's talk' is 이야기해요 or 대화해요; 의논하다 specifically aims at settling something.

english: to trust (firmly) / to have confidence in
usage: The trusted person/thing takes 을/를; 서로 frames it as firm, mutual confidence between parties.
신뢰할 수 있는 사람/회사 = a person/company you can trust; a common way to vouch for someone.
Set noun collocation: trust is something you 쌓다 (stack up) over time, then can 잃다 (lose).
신뢰 + 관계 is the standard compound for a trust-based bond in work, business, and diplomacy.
examples: 저는 그 사람을 신뢰해요.
I have confidence in that person.
Plain 을/를 object; note this sounds firmer and more formal than the everyday 믿어요.
저는 그 회사를 오래전부터 신뢰해 왔어요.
I've trusted that company for a long time.
신뢰해 오다 (have been trusting) shows confidence built up over time, typical for brands and institutions.
팀원들이 서로 신뢰해야 일이 잘 돼요.
Team members have to trust one another for work to go well.
Work register about reliability; 신뢰 here is reasoned, dependable confidence, not a fleeting hunch.
nuance: 신뢰하다 (信賴, '信 believe + 賴 rely') is firm, reasoned trust or confidence in a person, organization, or system, and it sounds notably more formal and weighty than the everyday verb 믿다 (to believe/trust). The dividing line is register and grounds: you 신뢰 a colleague's competence, a company, a brand, or a system on the basis of a track record, whereas you 믿다 a friend, a rumor, a promise, or a religion more casually and on faith. (믿다 also covers 'believe that…', which 신뢰하다 never does.) The trusted target takes 을/를, and the noun 신뢰 collocates richly: 신뢰를 쌓다 (build trust), 신뢰를 잃다 (lose trust), 신뢰 관계, 신뢰감. As a regular 하다-verb it is 신뢰해요 / 신뢰했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the 'big' word in casual speech: between close friends '나 믿지?' (you trust me, right?) is natural and warm, while 나 신뢰해? sounds stiff and oddly corporate — match 신뢰하다 to formal, reasoned, often written contexts and let 믿다 carry everyday emotional trust.

Marking the trusted target with 에게/한테 (그 사람에게 신뢰해요). What you trust is a direct object: 그 사람을 신뢰해요 — always 을/를.

usage: to give advice to a junior
The listener takes 에게/한테: 후배에게 / 친구한테 조언하다 — advice flows toward the receiver.
The topic takes 에 대해: N에 대해 조언하다 = advise about N; sounds knowledgeable and a touch formal.
The flip side from the receiver's view: 구하다 (seek) pairs with the noun 조언 to mean 'ask for advice'.
조언해 주다 frames the advice as a kindness; 주셔서 감사하다 is the standard polite thank-you.
examples: 친구에게 솔직하게 조언했어요.
I gave my friend honest advice.
에게 marks the receiver; 솔직하게 (honestly/frankly) is a natural adverb for candid counsel.
전문가가 건강 관리에 대해 조언해 줬어요.
An expert gave advice about managing your health.
N에 대해 조언해 주다: the 주다 helper frames it as a favor; sounds informed and slightly formal.
제가 조언할 입장은 아니지만 한번 들어 보세요.
I'm not really in a position to advise, but hear me out.
조언할 입장이 아니다 (not in a position to advise) is a humble hedge before offering an opinion.
nuance: 조언하다 (助言, '助 help + 言 words' — literally 'helping words') means to offer advice or counsel from knowledge or experience, and it sounds more thoughtful and a touch more formal than casually telling someone what to do. The key contrast is with 충고하다 (忠告): 조언 is helpful, supportive guidance you welcome, while 충고 carries a corrective, admonishing edge — closer to a warning or a talking-to ('너에게 충고하는데…' often precedes criticism), so they are not interchangeable in tone. It also differs from 추천하다 (recommend a specific thing) and 제안하다 (propose a course of action). Grammatically the listener takes 에게/한테 and the topic takes 에 대해; it lives as 조언해 주다 (give advice as a kindness) and the receiver's-side 조언을 구하다 (seek advice). As a 하다-verb it is 조언해요 / 조언했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the noun shape: English 'advise SOMEONE' tempts a direct object, but the person taught takes 에게/한테 (친구에게 조언해요), because what is actually 'given' is the 조언 itself — and note 조언 is uncountable-flavored, so 'a piece of advice' is 한마디 조언, not a pluralized form.

Using 조언하다 when you mean to warn or reproach. A corrective 'let me tell you for your own good' is 충고하다; 조언하다 is supportive guidance and softens the message.

usage: The topic takes 에 대해 or (으)로: 그 주제로 / 환경에 대해 토론하다 = debate the issue from sides.
찬반 (for-and-against) + 토론 names a structured debate with two opposing positions.
열띤 (heated, lively) is the signature modifier; 열띤 토론이 벌어졌다 = a heated debate broke out.
토론 + 회 (meeting) is the event noun: a panel or public forum held to debate an issue.
examples: 우리 그 주제로 한번 토론해요.
Let's have a debate on that topic.
Simple 요-form invite; (으)로 marks the topic, and 토론하다 implies weighing different sides, not chatting.
학생들이 환경 문제에 대해 토론했어요.
The students debated about environmental issues.
N에 대해 토론하다 = debate about N; presupposes presenting and weighing opposing arguments.
감정적으로 싸우지 말고 차분하게 토론합시다.
Let's not fight emotionally — let's debate calmly.
Contrasts 토론하다 (reasoned debate) with 싸우다 (quarrel); 토론 is meant to stay rational.
nuance: 토론하다 (討論, '討 examine + 論 argue') is to debate or discuss an issue formally, presenting and weighing different viewpoints, so it belongs to classrooms, panels, candidate debates, and structured meetings rather than casual chitchat. Place it among its neighbors: 토론하다 (argue a question from sides, often with opposing positions) is more confrontational and structured than 의논하다/상의하다 (talk something over together to decide), and entirely distinct from 대화하다 (just converse) and 싸우다 (quarrel) — a good 토론 stays reasoned even when heated. The topic takes 에 대해 or (으)로, it collocates with 열띤, 찬반, and 활발하게, and the noun appears in 토론회 (debate forum), 토론자 (debater), 끝장 토론 (a marathon, settle-it debate). As a regular 하다-verb it is 토론해요 / 토론했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is that English 'discuss' covers everything from a chat to a formal debate, so learners overuse 토론하다 for ordinary talk — if you just want to 'talk about' your weekend or 'chat' with a friend, say 이야기하다 or 대화하다; reserve 토론하다 for a genuine, argued exchange on an issue.
